title: I Backtested My XAUUSD EA for 20 Months: $300 → $19,743 — Tear It Apart
author: Party_Musician_9914
selftext:
I may get a little flack for posting this, but here goes...

I've been working on XAUUSD EAs for about four years now. I'm 62, I don't code, but I've always felt that I could eventually put together the right logic for an Expert Advisor if I kept at it long enough.

And I genuinely believe this may be the one.

Now, I know some people are going to look at the results and immediately say:

**"It's a backtest."**

Absolutely. I know that.

It's approximately 20 months of backtesting, and I fully understand that past backtest performance does not mean it's going to perform the same way going forward.

But I also think the actual numbers are worth looking at.

There were **101 baskets** in the test, with an **81.8% basket win rate**.

The loss distribution is one of the things that really caught my attention:

* 10 isolated single-basket losses
* 4 occurrences of two consecutive losing baskets
* No losing streak longer than two baskets
* 18 losing baskets in total
* A maximum winning streak of 19 consecutive baskets

That last number is pretty insane to me: **19 consecutive winning baskets.**

The EA trades multiple positions as a basket rather than treating every position as an independent trade. That's actually an idea I've had since long before ChatGPT.

Years ago, before any of these AI coding tools existed, I hired a developer from Cyprus to build my first EA around the concept. My thinking was that rather than relying on one position, I wanted to manage several positions together as one trade idea.

Over the years I've experimented with four positions, five positions and different basket structures. I've built some EAs that produced good results, but I've never felt quite as strongly about one as I do about this one.

For this particular experiment, I deliberately wanted to see what would happen if I made it **extremely aggressive**.

That's where the roughly **25% risk per basket** came from.

I'm NOT suggesting that 25% risk per basket is sensible conventional money management. It obviously isn't. 😂

I chose it specifically because of the historical loss distribution in the backtest. With no more than two consecutive losing baskets during this particular test, I wanted to see what the compounding would look like starting with a deliberately small account.

So I tested it starting with **$300**.

Over approximately 20 months, the backtest took that $300 to **$19,743**.

I also ran another experiment starting with only $200, simply because I wanted to see how far I could push the concept at very low starting balances.

Again, I completely understand the limitations here.

It's a backtest.

There will be slippage, spreads, execution differences, changing market conditions and potentially an entirely different distribution of wins and losses going forward. Even a relatively small degradation in performance matters enormously when you're talking about this level of risk.

But even allowing for a meaningful error margin, I think the underlying results are interesting enough to take seriously and investigate further.

I've spent about four years trying to build "the one" when it comes to XAUUSD.

Maybe this is it.

Maybe forward testing humbles me very quickly. 😂

Either way, I'm looking forward to finding out.

So... give me your feedback.

Challenge the backtest. Challenge the risk. Challenge the methodology. Point out something I may have overlooked.

Just look at the numbers as well.

I'm genuinely interested to hear what people think.

The 25% setting wasn’t presented as sensible long-term risk or something I would recommend using across all 101 trades. I deliberately pushed the EA to an extreme because I was trying to break it and see where the account, margin governor and compounding model failed. In real trading, who would responsibly continue risking 25% indefinitely as the account grew? Risk would be reduced and profits withdrawn. The exercise was a stress test of an aggressive small-account model, not a claim that two consecutive losses is the worst streak it will ever experience.

replies.author: Party_Musician_9914
replies.body: That’s a fair suggestion and exactly the kind of sequence-risk test this needs. The report contains 101 complete three-leg baskets—83 winners and 18 losers—with only a two-basket maximum losing streak in the historical order. I’ll run the Monte Carlo at basket level, not by shuffling the 303 individual legs. Each permutation also needs to recalculate percentage sizing, minimum-lot rounding and the three-leg margin governor from the changing balance; simply shuffling fixed dollar P/L would be misleading. I’ll report survival/ruin rate, drawdown percentiles, worst losing streaks, and how often the governor has to reduce or reject size.

replies.author: Party_Musician_9914
replies.body: You're exactly right that a Sharpe of 18 should stop anyone dead in their tracks if this were a standard portfolio simulation—but you're evaluating the wrong variable here. I wasn't running a standard 1% or 2% risk configuration meant to project long-term passive returns. I explicitly cranked the risk parameter to an extreme 25% per trade over a fast 101-trade run specifically to run a mechanical break-test on the script's core execution logic and see how low of a starting balance the code could survive. When you compress a highly accurate basket strategy into a high-leverage stress test, the variance drops to near-zero because the account either instantly blows up or spikes vertically, which temporarily forces a massive math anomaly in the Sharpe calculation. Dropping the risk to normal parameters naturally smooths out the curve and drops the ratio to normal levels, but the high-risk loop was an engineering break-test, not a passive backtest.

replies.author: Party_Musician_9914
replies.body:
Fair questions. The test was run on XAUUSD M5 from 1 January 2025 to 3 September 2026 using 99% real ticks. That was clearly a strong and unusually volatile period for gold, so I’m not treating one backtest as proof of a permanent or regime-independent edge.

The 25% basket risk was deliberately a small-account stress test, not an intended live-risk recommendation. The spectacular ending balance is therefore than the underlying questions: whether basket-level expectancy, profit factor and drawdown remain acceptable across older sideways, bearish and crisis periods.

The next has been developed through multiple filters and parameter tests, so parameter-selection bias is also a fair concern. The next I’m planning include 2015–2017, 2019–2020, rolling yearly slices, out-of-sample/walk-forward testing, parameter perturbation and Monte Carlo basket-order testing. I’ll publish both the successful and unsuccessful periods rather than presenting only the best window.

comments.author: MarcusDaughtry
comments.body:
Here’s my ai agents reply lol “THUNDERCLAW: Here’s a clean reply you could post:

Interesting work, but I think the biggest issue is that the backtest may be flattering the risk more than proving the edge.

A few things I’d want to know:

• 101 baskets over 20 months is not a huge sample  
• risking 25% per basket is extremely aggressive, so even a small change in loss distribution could wreck the curve  
• “no losing streak longer than 2 baskets” is exactly the kind of result I would not trust to hold up live  
• basket systems can sometimes hide averaging-down / martingale-type tail risk behind a pretty win rate

The first thing I’d test is robustness, not the headline return:

• out-of-sample period  
• Monte Carlo reshuffling of basket outcomes  
• spread/slippage stress  
• worse execution on gold during volatile periods  
• same logic at much lower risk, like 1-3% per basket

If the system is real, it should still look respectable after those tests. If it only looks magical at 25% risk with this exact historical sequence, then the backtest is probably telling a prettier story than reality will.

So my view is: promising enough to forward test, but nowhere near enough evidence yet to call it “the one.””

replies.author: Party_Musician_9914
replies.body:
That’s a fair assessment, and “promising but not proven” is close to my own position. A few important clarifications:

The 25% setting was deliberately an aggressive $300-account stress test of the sizing and margin-governor mechanics—not the risk I’m proposing for normal live trading.

It also isn’t averaging down, grid trading or martingale. All three legs open together from the same signal, with the same initial stop and no position added after price moves against the trade. They are simply divided into TP1, TP2 and a managed runner. Position size is not increased to recover a previous loss.

I agree that 101 baskets are encouraging but not conclusive, and I certainly don’t expect the historical maximum losing sequence of two to remain the live maximum. That is why basket-level Monte Carlo testing is next: the 101 complete baskets will be reordered thousands of times while recalculating percentage sizing, minimum-lot rounding and available margin after every result.

I also intend to test older and less favourable gold regimes, rolling time windows, spread/slippage deterioration, and materially lower risk. With a $300 balance, testing 1–3% properly may require a larger simulated balance or smaller contract specification because three broker-minimum 0.01-lot legs can create a risk floor above the requested percentage.

If the system deteriorates badly under those tests, that is valuable information rather than something to hide. If it remains profitable with tolerable drawdown, that will be much stronger evidence of edge than the headline 25% return.

So yes: an impressive stress-test result, but robustness and forward testing still have to earn the conclusion.

replies.author: Party_Musician_9914
replies.body:
That’s a good warning. This particular test was already run using “Every tick based on real ticks” with 99% history quality, rather than generated ticks or an OHLC model.

An equally important piece of context is that it was deliberately run at an extreme 25% target risk per three-leg basket on a $300 account. That was a stress test of the margin governor and all-leg execution—not a risk level I would consider appropriate for normal live trading. It massively amplifies both returns and drawdowns.

The 25% setting does not automatically create a profitable strategy or manufacture profit factor, because PF compares gross profit with gross loss. However, compounding, minimum-lot rounding and margin-based volume reductions can affect the result indirectly, so it still needs to be retested at realistic risk levels.

Real ticks are a much stronger starting point, but they still cannot reproduce every aspect of live execution. Slippage, latency, changing spreads, commissions and broker differences will be included in the next stress tests. Do you remember which modelling mode produced your original PF 6 result?
